Loops — Session 12

The one idea to landA while loop has three controlling lines in three different places — the initialization before it sets the counter, the termination condition on the loop line is asked again before every pass, and the updation inside the body changes what that condition looks at. Leave any of the three out and the loop runs forever, or the wrong number of times, or not at all.

Recap — what stuck from nested conditions · Slide 3

Slide 3Nested Conditions
Recap — three questions

Recap · Nested Conditional Statements

Three Questions

What does this print?

a = 7
b = 4
if a > b:
    if b > 5:
        print("both")
    print("outer")
print("done")
  • both, outer, done
  • outer, done
  • done
  • nothing at all

2 — outer, then done. The outer if passes, so Python goes in. The if inside it asks 4 > 5, which is False, so that print is never reached.if a > b: True if b > 5: False print("both") print("outer")print("done")Blue = Python ran it. Faded = never even read.

And this one?

marks = 85
if marks >= 91:
    print("A")
elif marks >= 81:
    print("B")
elif marks >= 71:
    print("C")
  • B
  • B and C
  • C
  • A, B and C

1 — B, and only B. Once one rung of an if-elif chain is True, every rung below it is skipped without ever being tested.if marks >= 91: Falseelif marks >= 81: True print("B")elif marks >= 71: print("C")71 was never even looked at.

What appears on the screen?

age = 15
if age >= 18:
    print("Can vote")
  • Can vote
  • nothing at all
  • False
  • an error

2 — nothing at all. There is no else, so when the condition is False there is simply nothing left to run. A program with no output is not a broken program.if age >= 18: False print("Can vote")Hold on to this one. It comes back at the end of today.

While Loop

Name the Three Parts

Page 1, task 2. One program you have not seen. In the margin beside it, write the word — the actual word — against the line it belongs to:

  • Write initialization beside the line that sets the counter before the loop starts.
  • Write termination condition beside the line that decides whether the loop runs again.
  • Write updation beside the line that changes the counter.
  • Then answer the one question under it: how many times does line 4 run?

Hands-on — type it, then break it

Hands-on — type it, then break it

While Loop

Type It, Then Break It

Type this into the playground exactly as it is. The first line asks for a. Give it a = 5 and run. Then run it again with a = 1, and again with a = 100.

a = int(input())
counter = 0
while counter < 3:
    a = a + 1
    print(a)
    counter = counter + 1
print("End")

I think I have left a line out of that program by mistake. Delete the line counter = counter + 1 and run it again with a = 5.

The stop button is beside Run. You are going to need it.

Put the line back. Now move it above print(a) and run with a = 5 again. What changed, and what did not?

While Loop

Before You Go

A name-board app prints one letter of a name per line. Somebody types a single letter: R. What appears on the screen?

1  a = input()
2  counter = 0
3  length_of_a = len(a)
4  while counter < (length_of_a - 1):
5      print(a[counter])
6      counter = counter + 1
  • R
  • nothing at all
  • IndexError: string index out of range
  • R, over and over, forever

2 — nothing at all. len("R") is 1, so line 4 asks 0 < 0, which is False the very first time. The body never runs once.counter = 0length_of_a = 1while 0 < (1 - 1): False print(a[counter]) counter = counter + 1Nothing on screen, and nothing wrong with the machine.

Checkpoint 1 — they can say what a loop is for

Opening · 1 min · slide 1 of 29

Name the session and nothing else

How it goes
  1. Title up before you say anything: “Loops.”
  2. One line only: “yesterday we decided whether a line runs. Today we decide how many times it runs.”
  3. Hand straight over: “first, what stuck from yesterday?”
  • Do not start the agenda here. The agenda comes after the hook.

Watch for Nothing yet. This slide is ten seconds.

Recap · 4 min · slide 2 of 29

The shape from last session, on one slide

How it goes
  1. Put it up and say the name: “nested conditions — an if inside an if.”
  2. Read the picture, do not re-teach it: condition A holds the whole orange block, and condition B holds only block 2 inside it.
  3. One question to the room: “if condition A is False, does Python ever look at condition B?” Wait for no.
  4. Hand over: “three questions on it, and then we start today.”
  • Forty seconds on this slide. It is a reminder, not a lesson.
  • If the room is blank here, do not reteach — the three questions will tell you how bad it is, and you can open tomorrow with it.

Watch for Nothing to watch yet. The poll on the next card is the measurement.

Recap poll · 4 min · slide 3 of 29

Three questions from last session

How it goes
  1. Read Q1 aloud and let them read the code. The timer starts by itself — do not talk over it.
  2. Count hands option by option: “hands for 1… for 2… for 3… for 4.” Say out loud that a closed fist is a real answer you want to see.
  3. Press Reveal. Walk the little trace beside it: blue is what Python ran, faded is what it never even read.
  4. Say why each wrong option is tempting before you move on — 1 is “I assumed both ifs get asked”, 3 is “I lost the outer block”.
  5. Q2 and Q3 the same way, briskly. On Q3 add one line: “remember that — a program that prints nothing.”
  • Next / Back step the three questions. Reveal is a separate press.
  • Do not discuss. Three questions, three minutes, move.

Watch for A big vote for Q2 option 2 means the elif chain has not landed. Note it; do not stop and reteach.

Hook · 4 min · slide 4 of 29

Behind the scenes at the xerox machine

How it goes
  1. Start from something all of them have done: “the xerox shop outside the gate. You hand over one form and say forty copies.”
  2. Say what they already know, so nobody has to correct you: “he does not press the button forty times. He types 40, presses START once, and goes back to his phone.”
  3. Now the question that is actually interesting: “but the machine only knows how to make one copy. So what is happening inside it, forty times over?” Take two or three answers. Take the wrong ones too. Correct nobody.
  4. Press once. The red brace appears: “one job, forty times over. That is all the machine is doing.”
  5. Ask before the last press: “and if he had typed four hundred?” Wait for the groan.
  6. Press again. Say nothing at all while it moves. Then: “one instruction, written once. Forty copies still come out.”
  7. Hand over: “that shape has a name, and it is today.”
  • Three presses total. Replay if the room missed the collapse — it is worth a second run.
  • Arrow keys step it in presenter view.
  • Do not claim the operator presses the button forty times. They know he does not, and the hook dies the moment one of them says so.

Watch for If somebody says “loop” before you do, take it and use their word all session.

Your turn · 3 min · slide 5 of 29

Where else does one press repeat a job?

How it goes
  1. Carry it straight over from the machine: “one press, and it repeats the same small job until it has done it enough times. Where else have you seen that?”
  2. Then stop talking. The silence is doing the work — do not fill it with your own example.
  3. Take four. Make each one say both halves: the machine, and the one job it repeats. “ATM” is half an answer; “the ATM counts one note, again and again, until it reaches the amount” is the answer.
  4. Repeat each one back in their words and write it on the board. Do not judge any of them.
  5. Hand off by picking one: “somebody said the ATM — hold that one.”
  • If the room is silent after ten seconds, name one from this campus — the ATM counting out notes, the water cooler filling a bottle, the attendance app sending the same SMS to sixty parents, IRCTC checking seats once a second — and ask who else has one.
  • Never go round naming people. Keep the four on the board; they come back at the takeaways.

Watch for Answers that describe one big job rather than one small job repeated. Ask the follow-up: “and how many times does it do that?”

Agenda · 3 min · slide 6 of 29

The four stops, and the sheets

How it goes
  1. Straight on from their examples: “here is the route.”
  2. Read the four stops off the picture: Loops, While Loop, Code Walkthrough, and the Common Mistakes hanging above it.
  3. One promise: “by the end you will have written one of these yourself.”
  4. Then hand out the sheets and set the next task going.
  • Hand out all three worksheet pages now, face down, one set per student. This is the only hand-out moment in the session.
  • Ten seconds per stop. Do not narrate the sub-labels.

Watch for Nothing. This slide exists so the room knows where it is going.

Checkpoint 2 — they can point at the line that repeats

Paper 1 · 5 min · slide 7 of 29 · worksheet page 1

Ten numbers, the long way

How it goes
  1. Turn the sheets over. Page 1, task 1 has the three-number program already printed.
  2. Read the change once: “same question, but now it asks for the next ten.”
  3. Say the two things they write: the lines they would add, and then the two numbers in the little table.
  4. Press play on the timer. Three minutes.
  5. Walk the rows while they work and keep talking to them — “are you guys done?” · “come on, let us see who finishes first” · “one minute left, just the line count now”.
  6. Pens down. Ask for the line count by show of hands: “fewer than fifteen? … more than twenty?” Then: “and for a hundred numbers?”
  • Press play on the timer. It does not start by itself.
  • Do not show a solution. The next slides are the answer.
  • Task 2 is on the same page. Tell them to leave it alone for now.

Watch for Twenty-one lines is right (one input line plus ten pairs). Anyone who wrote a loop already has been reading ahead — ask them to hold it for two slides.

Concept · 3 min · slide 8 of 29

A loop runs a block several times

How it goes
  1. Open from their own sheets: “twenty-one lines, and you all wrote the same two of them ten times.”
  2. Now name it, pointing at the orange arrow: “a loop lets us execute one block of code several times.”
  3. Check them with a question, do not tell: “how many different lines are in that blue block? One block, how many runs?”
  4. Offer doubts: “any doubts here?”
  • Do not name while or for yet. The next slide does that, and it lands better as an answer.

Watch for If the room is quiet at the check question, narrow it: “point at the block that repeats.”

Concept · 3 min · slide 9 of 29

Python has two ways to loop

How it goes
  1. Ask first: “so how do we write one in Python?” Then put the slide up.
  2. Read it plainly: two primary ways — the while loop and the for loop.
  3. Say which is which and when: “today is while, start to finish. For is tomorrow. Both do the same job; they are written differently.”
  4. Do not compare them. One sentence about for, then move.
  • Twenty seconds. Its only job is that nobody leaves thinking while is the only loop there is.
  • If somebody asks which is better, say: “neither. You pick by what you are counting, and you will know that by tomorrow evening.”

Watch for Students who have seen for loops elsewhere will want to use one all session. Tell them plainly that today is about the three lines you have to write yourself.

Concept · 2 min · slide 10 of 29

The while shape

How it goes
  1. Straight on: “this is the first one, and it is called while.”
  2. Read the shape off the picture in order — the word while, the condition, the colon, and then the indented block underneath it.
  3. Connect it to yesterday out loud: “same colon, same indent as an if. The difference is one word.”
  4. Then the difference that matters: “an if asks its condition once. This one asks it again, every time round.”
  5. Hand over with the line that sets up the next four slides: “so let us see how your ten-numbers problem gets solved with one of these.”
  • Point at the indent with your hand. That is the same rule they learned yesterday.

Watch for A student saying “so it is an if that repeats” has it. Use their sentence.

Checkpoint 3 — they can name the three parts on any loop

Build 1 of 4 · 6 min · slide 11 of 29

Initialization — the line before the loop

How it goes
  1. Frame the whole run of four first: “we are going to build this program one line at a time. Four slides. Watch where each new line goes.”
  2. Point at what is already there: the input, the while line with its condition still blank, and the two lines from their own sheet that repeat.
  3. Now the new line, and ask before you read it: “if I want this to happen exactly three times, what do I need first?” Take it from the room. Somebody will say “count”.
  4. Read the label out loud and write it on the board: initialization. Counter equals zero.
  5. One check: “why zero? How many times has the block run when Python reaches this line?”
  • Write initialization, termination condition and updation on the board as they arrive. Leave all three there for the rest of the session.
  • Ninety seconds on this slide.

Watch for The common wrong answer to “why zero” is “because counting starts at one”. Push once: “how many copies have come out before the machine starts?”

Build 2 of 4 · 6 min · slide 12 of 29

Updation — the line inside that changes it

How it goes
  1. Ask before showing: “we have a counter sitting at zero. Who is going to change it?”
  2. Let them answer, then point at the new green line. Read the label: updation.
  3. The question that matters here is where it lives: “is that line inside the loop or outside it? How can you tell?” Wait for the indent.
  4. Say it once, plainly: “nothing else in this program touches counter. If that line is not there, counter stays zero forever.”
  • Ninety seconds. Keep your hand on the indent while they answer.
  • Do not mention infinite loops yet. They discover that themselves on their own machines.

Watch for Anyone reading updation as part of the output. Ask: “does that line print anything?”

Build 3 of 4 · 6 min · slide 13 of 29

Now you write the condition

How it goes
  1. This slide is a question, so ask it and then stop talking: “what should the condition be?”
  2. Ten seconds of silence. Then take answers from three different parts of the room before you say whether any of them is right.
  3. Push on whatever they give you: “counter equals three?” — “when would that be True? Walk it with me.”
  4. Do not resolve it here. “Hold your answer. Next slide.”
  • Resist filling the silence. This is the only slide in the build where they do the work.
  • Sixty seconds, most of it quiet.

Watch for A room that offers counter < 3 straight away is ahead — ask that student why three and not two, and let the rest hear the reasoning.

Build 4 of 4 · 6 min · slide 14 of 29

Termination condition, and the whole program

How it goes
  1. Reveal it: counter less than three. Then check it against their answers, not against the slide.
  2. Walk the values out loud and make them finish it: “counter is 0, is 0 less than 3? Yes. 1? Yes. 2? Yes. 3? …” Let the room say no. That is three runs.
  3. Read the label: termination condition. Then the sentence that carries the session: “this line is not read once. It is read again before every single pass.”
  4. Step back and name all three together, pointing: initialization above, termination condition on the while line, updation at the bottom of the body.
  5. Offer doubts. These three words come back every time for the rest of the course.
  • Two minutes. This is the payoff slide of the run of four.
  • Say “termination condition” in full at least twice. They need the exact words on the sheet in a moment.

Watch for The common wrong answer on “why three” is “because we want three”. Push once: “yes, but count the yeses with me.”

Concept · 2 min · slide 15 of 29

The shape, with the names on it

How it goes
  1. Straight on: “strip the example away and this is what is left. This is every while loop you will ever write.”
  2. Read it top to bottom: initialization outside, termination condition on the while line, block of code indented, updation last and still indented.
  3. One check: “which of those four is outside the loop?” Wait for it.
  4. Hand over: “pens. I want you to find these three on a program you have not seen.”
  • This is the diagram they will redraw in the exam, and it is the one the takeaways map rebuilds at the end. Leave it up while you give the task.

Watch for Anyone pointing at updation as outside has confused the indent. Fix it here, not later.

Paper 2 · 4 min · slide 16 of 29 · worksheet page 1

Name the three parts

How it goes
  1. Page 1, task 2. One program, and they have not seen this one.
  2. Read the three marks off the panel slowly, and say the words in full: they write initialization, termination condition and updation in the margin beside the right line. Not a circle, not a box — the word.
  3. Do the first one together, out loud, so nobody is guessing at the verb.
  4. Press play. Two and a half minutes. Walk the rows — “any doubts about the task? Ask now” · “one minute, and the question underneath”.
  5. Pens down first. Then say the check, not before: every loop you will ever write has exactly one of each. If you have written a word twice, look again.
  6. Take the three answers by show of hands, one word at a time. Then the number.
  • Press play on the timer.
  • Say the self-check only after pens are down. Printed on the sheet it would be a hint.

Watch for The answers are line 2, line 3 and line 6, and line 4 runs five times. The condition uses <= rather than <, which is the bit worth twenty seconds: “counter starts at 1 and the test is less-than-or-equal. Count the yeses.”

Explainer · 4 min · slide 17 of 29

Ask it again — follow the dot

How it goes
  1. Open from the marks they just made: “you found the three lines. Now watch what Python does with them.”
  2. The slider is set to 2. Before you touch anything: “write down what this prints. All of it.” Ten seconds, on the corner of page 1.
  3. Press Play, then narrate the dot as it moves — one step per sentence, asking rather than telling: “first it sets a to 5, and counter to 0. Now it reaches the diamond. Is 0 less than 2? Yes, so we go inside. a becomes 6. We print a. Now counter becomes 1 …”
  4. Then, with your hand on the back edge: “and look where it goes next. Back up to the same question. Is 1 less than 2? Yes again. In we go …”
  5. On the pass that fails, slow right down: “counter is 2. Is 2 less than 2? No. So we do not go in. We come out at the bottom and print End.”
  6. Now drag the slider to 0 and ask before playing: “what prints now?” Take the vote. Most of the room says 6.
  7. Play it. The whole body greys out and stays grey. “Not once. The block ran zero times, and that is not a bug.”
  • One step is the button to use while you narrate — it stops on the line they argued about.
  • Press Reset before you leave the slide, or the next class sees a finished run.

Watch for The 0 prediction is the one that splits the room. Let them be wrong out loud before you play it.

Checkpoint 4 — they can say why a loop never stops

Hands-on · 8 min · slide 18 of 29

Type it, then break it

How it goes
  1. Laptops open. “Type this exactly. Do not copy mine — type it.” The first line asks for a, so run it with a = 5, then a = 1, then a = 100. Four minutes; nine lines with this many people is not one minute.
  2. Walk the rows. Most errors will be the indent or the colon. Say so out loud once so nobody feels singled out.
  3. Step to panel 2 and frame it as your own mistake: “I think I have left a line out by accident — delete counter equals counter plus one and run it again with a = 5.” Do not warn them.
  4. Let them react. Somebody will shout. Only then: “what is it waiting for? Counter is still zero, so the answer to the question never changes.”
  5. Show them the stop button once, then step to panel 3: put the line back, and move it above print(a).
  6. Take the difference from the room: “same three numbers? No — what changed?”
  • Panels 1, 2, 3 step with Next. Each has its own timer; press play on each.
  • Know where the stop button is in your playground before the session.
  • This beat is the fourth common mistake — not updating the counter — and they meet it by doing it, not on a slide. That is why it is not on the sheet later.

Watch for Moving the update above print(a) prints 6, 7, 8 still — counter is not printed. The lesson is that order inside the body matters for what prints, not for how many passes.

Paper 3 · 6 min · slide 19 of 29 · worksheet page 2

Find the mistake

How it goes
  1. Open from what they just did: “you broke updation on purpose. Here are three programs somebody broke by accident.”
  2. Page 2. Say the shape of the task once: three programs, one wrong line in each, and each one is wrong in a different part.
  3. Say the three things they write: circle the line, name the part, and say what happens when you run it. Read the inputs off the sheet — 5, then 10, then 1.
  4. Press play. Five minutes. Laptops closed for this one, and say why: running them answers the question for free.
  5. Walk the rows. “Which part is that? Say the word” · “programme 3 is the sneaky one — count the yeses”.
  6. Pens down. Do not take the answers here — the next three slides are the answers, one at a time.
  • Press play on the timer.
  • Keep laptops shut. If somebody runs programme 2 they freeze their tab, and you lose the reveal.
  • Answers, for you only: programme 1 has no initialization; programme 2 stores the answer of the condition in a box; programme 3 starts the counter at 1 and runs twice, not three times.

Watch for Programme 3 is the one most of them will mark correct. That is the finding, and it is worth saying out loud when the reveal comes.

Reveal 1 of 3 · 4 min · slide 20 of 29

Missing initialization

How it goes
  1. Programme 1 first. Ask for hands before you show anything: “who circled line 2?”
  2. Then reveal, and read the error text out exactly: name counter is not defined.
  3. Ask them to name the part: “which of the three is missing?” Take the word from the room, not from you.
  4. Say the rule they can use in an exam: “if you ever see that error under a while loop, look above the loop, not inside it.”
  • Eighty seconds. It is the easy one of the three.

Watch for Students often read NameError as a typo. Say plainly it is not spelling — the line that creates the variable is simply not there.

Reveal 2 of 3 · 4 min · slide 21 of 29

A condition stored in a box

How it goes
  1. Programme 2. Hands first: “who circled line 3? Who circled line 4?” Both are defensible — say so.
  2. Read line 3 aloud very slowly: condition equals, bracket, counter less than three, bracket.
  3. Ask the one question and then stop talking: “what gets stored in condition — the question, or the answer?”
  4. Now the slide: the answer, True, stored once. Line 4 asks the box, not the counter. Line 7 keeps changing counter, and nothing ever looks at counter again.
  5. Name it: infinite loop. Then connect it back: “same ending as when you deleted the update line. Different cause.”
  • Ninety seconds. This is the hard one of the three.
  • Call the variable “the box called condition” every time, or the sentence becomes unparseable.

Watch for Two different causes, one symptom. If a student conflates them, ask: “which line was wrong in each?”

Reveal 3 of 3 · 4 min · slide 22 of 29

Off by one

How it goes
  1. Programme 3 last, and ask the honest question: “how many of you marked this one correct?” Count the hands. It will be most of the room.
  2. Point at the output: input is 1, three numbers were wanted, two came out.
  3. Walk the counter out loud with them: starts at 1, so 1 yes, 2 yes, 3 no. Two passes.
  4. Give them both repairs: start at 0 and keep less than 3, or start at 1 and use less than 4. Ask which they prefer and why.
  5. Close the set: “initialization, termination condition, updation. You have now broken all three and seen what each one costs.”
  • This is the mistake that will cost them marks in an exam. Say that out loud.
  • Ninety seconds, and the count of hands at the start is the point of it.

Watch for Anyone who says “just change it to 4” is right and should be asked to say why it works — that is the understanding you want.

Hard floor — exit runs whatever else is dropped

Concept · 2 min · slide 23 of 29

The square pattern

How it goes
  1. Read the question off the slide: stars in N rows and N columns, and for an input of 4 the output is four rows of four.
  2. Point at the output and say the thing that costs marks: there is a space after every star.
  3. Give them the shortcut they already own: “which string operation gives you a star and a space, n times?” Take string repetition from the room.
  4. Ask, and hold the answer: “which part repeats — the row, or the star?” They decide it on the sheet.
  • Do not code this on screen. They write it.
  • Say the space rule twice. It is the single most common reason a correct program fails a test case here. If nobody recalls string repetition, write "* " * 3 on the board and let them read it.

Watch for A room that says “both” is ahead of the syllabus — tell them they are right, and that the inner one has a shortcut today.

Hands-on · 7 min · slide 24 of 29 · worksheet page 3

Write it yourself

How it goes
  1. Page 3. Only the first line is given. Everything after is theirs.
  2. Say the order plainly: “sheet first, then keyboard. If you type first you will guess, and I will not be able to help you.”
  3. Press play. Five minutes. Walk the rows continuously — “are you guys done?” · “show me your three parts” · “two minutes — get it typed”.
  4. For anyone stuck, ask the three words, do not give code: “where is your initialization?”
  5. Last ninety seconds: everybody types and checks with 3, then 5, then 1.
  • Press play on the timer.
  • Do not put a solution on screen while they work.

Watch for The common bug is counter less than 3 hard-coded instead of counter less than n — it passes their first test and fails the second. Let them find it with input 5.

Concept · 2 min · slide 25 of 29

The solution

How it goes
  1. Up on screen only after the timer has run out.
  2. Read it against their three words: initialization, termination condition using n, the block, updation.
  3. Point at the line that does the work: print of star-space times n, inside a loop that runs n times. “The star repeats across with the string. The row repeats down with the loop.”
  4. Ask for hands: “who got the same three parts, even if your variable names are different?”
  • Do not retype it. Compare it to what is already on their screens.
  • This is exactly the program their sheet asks for, line for line. A student who stored the row in a variable first is also correct — say so out loud.

Watch for Anyone whose program works for 4 but not 5 hard-coded the number. Name the symptom, not the student.

Takeaways · 3 min · slide 26 of 29

The map, one press at a time

How it goes
  1. Do not read it out. Ask for it. Press 1 gives them the word loops; then ask “and how many kinds did we see?” before press 2.
  2. Press 2: while and for. One line only — “today was this one. Tomorrow is that one.”
  3. Presses 3 to 6 rebuild the block diagram from slide 15, one band at a time. Ask for each word before you press: “what goes above the loop? What goes on the while line? What goes at the bottom of the body?”
  4. Press 6 also draws the arrow back up. Point at it: “and that is the bit that surprised you — it asks again.”
  5. Press 7: “and if you leave one out?” They have broken all three today, so take it from them.
  6. Close: “one question, and then you can go.”
  • Seven presses. Arrow keys work in presenter view.
  • If the room is quiet, press and read — but ask first.

Watch for They should be able to produce all three words unprompted. If they cannot, that is what opens tomorrow.

Exit · 4 min · slide 27 of 29

One question, and it is hard

How it goes
  1. Frame it as a real thing: “a name-board app prints one letter per line. Somebody types a single letter.”
  2. Read the code once, by line number. Then stop talking and press play on the timer. Two and a half minutes, silent.
  3. Vote by hands, option by option. Count every option out loud.
  4. Reveal. Walk it: length is 1, so the question is 0 less than 0, which is False the first time. The body never runs.
  5. Name each wrong option: 1 is “a loop must run at least once”, 3 is “I saw an index and expected an index error”, 4 is “I saw a while and expected forever”.
  6. Close: “take that same program home and run it with your own name in it. Tomorrow is the for loop.”
  • Press play on the timer. It does not start by itself.
  • This runs even if everything else is cut. It is the hard floor.

Watch for A big vote for option 1 is the finding worth carrying into tomorrow: they still believe a loop body always runs once.

Closing · 1 min · slide 28 of 29

Feedback

How it goes
  1. Put it up while they are still packing, and say where the form is: “the feedback link is under today’s session. Thirty seconds, and it is anonymous.”
  2. Ask for one specific thing rather than a rating: “tell me the one minute of today that was too fast.”
  • Twenty seconds. Do not read the form out.
  • Say it before they stand up, not after.

Watch for Nothing to watch. If nobody fills it in, ask for one sentence on paper at the door instead.

Closing · 1 min · slide 29 of 29

Thank you

How it goes
  1. Last slide, and one sentence: “tomorrow, the for loop — the same three parts, written in one line.”
  2. Then let them go.
  • Ten seconds. Do not start a new idea on this slide.

Watch for Nothing. Watch the door instead.

Common guidelines

Things true of every slide

Never start a slide cold

Every slide opens from something the room already has — the sheet in their hand, the program on their screen, the answer somebody just gave. If a slide feels abrupt, the fix is one sentence at the end of the previous slide, not a longer explanation on this one.

Walk it in steps, and check as you go

Do not deliver a finished explanation. Say one step, then ask the next as a question — “so counter is 3 now. Is 3 less than 3? No, right? Good.” If the room does not answer, you have found the gap for free. Offer doubts out loud, often; it costs four seconds.

How every poll runs

Let them read and think first. Then count the hands option by option, out loud, including the options nobody picked. Say once, at the start of the session, that a closed fist means “not sure” and that it is a real answer you want to see. Reveal. Then explain every option, not just the right one — the wrong ones are where the misconceptions live.

Picking students

Call a row or a side of the room, never a name. Rotate which group you call. Never name a student who got something wrong, and never say whose screen you are looking at.

When nobody answers

Count ten seconds in your head. Then narrow the question rather than answering it: “point at the line that repeats” is answerable when “what do you notice?” is not.

Why paper before the keyboard

The keyboard is the marking scheme, not the exercise. A student who predicts on paper and then runs it finds out they were wrong; a student who types first finds out nothing, because the machine answered before they committed.

Say the three words in full, every time

Initialization, termination condition, updation. Not “the first bit”, not “the check”, not “the plus one”. The sheet asks them to write the words out, the exam will use the words, and the whole session is built so that by the takeaways they can produce all three unprompted.

Two words that mean different things today

Say “the termination condition” for the test on the while line, and “the counter” for the variable. Never say “the value” for either. In programme 2 of the mistake hunt there is also a variable named condition — call that one “the box called condition” every time, or the sentence becomes unparseable.

Reading the room

Pens still moving after the timer means the task was too long — take the next one down by a minute. Laptops closed during a paper beat is the beat working. Nobody looking up during a hands-on means they are stuck, not busy; walk and look. A student rerunning the same code unchanged has not read the error. Laughter on the break-it beat is the beat landing.

If you are short of time

Take the mistake hunt down from five minutes of writing to three and go straight to the reveals. Shorten the write-it-yourself beat to five minutes before you touch anything else. Drop the feedback and thank-you slides, which cost a minute between them. Never drop the exit question or the dot.

If they ask

  • “Can I use a for loop instead?” Yes, and that is tomorrow. Today the point is the three lines you have to write yourself.
  • “Which is better, while or for?” Neither. You pick by what you are counting, and you will be able to choose by tomorrow evening.
  • “Does the counter have to be called counter?” No. Call it i, or count, or anything. The name has no meaning to Python.
  • “Can the counter go down instead of up?” Yes — start at 3 and use counter > 0 with counter = counter - 1. Same three parts.
  • “What if the condition is never False?” The program runs until you stop it. That is the infinite loop, and it is not an error message — nothing is wrong as far as Python is concerned.
  • “Why is print("End") not indented?” Same rule as yesterday: the indent says which block a line belongs to. Outdented means it is outside the loop, so it runs once, after.
  • “My infinite loop froze the playground.” Stop button beside Run. If the tab is unresponsive, reload it — the code is saved.
